episodes.title: Google Sheets Filter Changed Everyone's View? Use THIS #Shorts
episodes.source_linked_claims: Filter views can apply to only one user's view of shared Sheet
scenes: A normal Google Sheets filter can affect what collaborators see. A filter view is useful when you want your own view.
Google's help explains filter views let you sort and filter without changing another person's view of the spreadsheet.
In Google Sheets on a computer, open Data and create a filter view. Menu names may vary by version.
Give the filter view a descriptive name so you can use it again. You can also share its link.
Filtering hides rows from your selected view; it does not erase their data. Double-check before deleting anything.

episodes.title: Google Sheets Protected Range Is NOT a Security Lock #Shorts
episodes.source_linked_claims: Protected ranges limit editing, not a security boundary; copies and exporting remain possible
scenes: A protected Google Sheets range can limit editing, but Google warns that protection is not a security measure.
In Data, Protect sheets and ranges, you can choose who is allowed to edit a particular area.
A warning is not an editing block. Choose Restrict who can edit if you need an actual editing limit.
Google notes that people with access may still be able to copy or export protected spreadsheet content.
Use protection to prevent accidental edits, not to hide secrets. Share sensitive sheets only with people you trust.

episodes.title: Google Sheets Shared with a Team? Avoid These 5 Filter & Permission Mistakes
episodes.source_linked_claims: Google Sheets Filter View and Protect sheets and ranges official help
scenes: Imagine a fictional team spreadsheet where one collaborator applies a regular filter and other people suddenly see fewer rows. No records were deleted, but the shared view changed. Let's make collaboration less confusing.
Google explains that a standard filter can be visible to people with access to the same Sheet. If your filter hides rows, collaborators may wonder whether their records have disappeared.
Use a Filter View when you want to sort and filter your own view without changing what others see. Google Sheets supports saved, named filter views for different ways to inspect the same data.
On a computer, choose Data and Create filter view in Google Sheets. Apply your conditions, save the view, and give it a descriptive name. Interface labels can differ between product versions.
You can also copy the URL of an applied filter view and share that view with a collaborator. A link to a filter view is not the same as giving someone new edit access to the spreadsheet.
Filtering changes what rows you see; it is not an instruction to delete the hidden records. Before removing any data, clear the filter and verify the full source range is intact.

In team workbooks, a collaborator might overwrite a formula cell or dashboard total. Restricting edits to important ranges can help prevent accidental changes while leaving intended input cells editable.
Google Sheets lets you open Data, Protect sheets and ranges, choose a range or sheet and set who can edit. Review those permissions for each protected area instead of relying on a warning message.
A warning before editing is not the same as restricting who may edit. Google provides both options. If the aim is to prevent edits by other collaborators, use the correct restriction option.
Protected ranges are not security boundaries. Google explicitly warns people may still copy or export spreadsheet contents. Restrict editing only solves editing risks, not data confidentiality.

Before distributing an important report, check file-sharing roles. Give editor access only to trusted collaborators who need to modify the document. Use viewer or commenter access for people who do not need to edit.

Use filter views for individual analysis, protect important formulas against unwanted edits, and manage actual access through sharing permissions. The best collaboration setup makes each person's task easy without hiding or exposing the wrong information.
